title: Al-Azhar in Cairo
hookLine: the mosque and university founded by the Fatimids, later a great center of Sunni learning

lines: A RING OF STUDENTS BY A PILLAR.
A GREAT MOSQUE FOR A NEW CITY.
cards: A student sits on a mat with his back against a stone column. A teacher sits against the next column over, a small ring of students around him. Another ring sits by the next pillar, and another by the one after that.
Nobody has a desk. Some have a book on their knees, some only their memory. That's a class in this mosque: a circle on the floor, beside a pillar.
The new city by the Nile needed a great mosque, and its builders raised one close to the palaces: al-Azhar.

teach.b: Al-Azhar was built by the Fatimids, the Isma'ili dynasty from yesterday.

Tradition explains the name as the radiant, or the shining one, and some connect it with Fatimah al-Zahra, the daughter of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, from whom the Fatimids traced their line.
Scholars give that link with a little caution, and so will i. At first it taught the Isma'ili teaching of its founders.

Later, when the Fatimid age ended and new rulers held Egypt, the mosque came to teach Sunni learning, and became one of the places Sunni students traveled toward: the Qur'an, hadith, law, Arabic grammar, the sciences that serve the text.

One building, two chapters of Islamic history, neither one ranked. Why travel so far to sit on a mat by a pillar? The Qur'an has a short prayer for that kind of hunger, one it teaches the Prophet to say.

teach.h: MY LORD! INCREASE ME IN KNOWLEDGE.
teach.b: In Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge." Not wealth, not fame. Knowledge.
Learning happened in a mosque, between the prayers; a class could stop for the call to prayer and pick up again after.

teach.h: A TEACHER, A PILLAR, A CIRCLE.
teach.b: And the method was the circle. A teacher read, explained and answered. Students copied, memorized, questioned, and when a teacher judged a student ready, gave permission to teach in turn.
People today speak of al-Azhar as a thousand years of study. Whatever the exact count, the picture holds: someone, by a pillar, reading.

how: Al-Azhar is still a working mosque and a place of Islamic learning in Cairo, and students study the Qur'an, hadith, law and Arabic there, some in circles around a teacher.

games.q: you're a student who has traveled far to Cairo. there are many teachers in the mosque, each by a different pillar. what do you do?
o: wait for a classroom with desks to open.
join a ring on the floor by a pillar.
study alone from books you brought.
games.why: you sit down in a circle. the teacher reads and explains, students copy, memorize and ask, and the class pauses for prayer.

practice: Sit as if you've just joined a ring on the floor, and bring to mind one thing you've been meaning to understand better: a verse, a word, a question about this path. Hold the question, not the answer: what exactly don't you know?
If you pray, you can say the line the Qur'an teaches, My Lord! Increase me in knowledge; if you don't, let the question sit quietly.
